title: Febrile Neutropenia
subject: Medicine
summary: Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency defined by fever and an absolute neutrophil count <500/µL. Prompt assessment, risk stratification and empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Fever (single oral temperature ≥38.3 °C or ≥38.0 °C sustained for ≥1 h) plus an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <500/µL, or <1000/µL with a predicted decline to <500 within 48 h, defines febrile neutropenia.
b: ANC = WBC × % neutrophils (including bands) ÷ 100
Use a calibrated thermometer; in low‑resource settings a reliable digital device suffices

t.b: Confirms neutropenia; ANC <500 µL confirms diagnosis
Identifies fever; ≥38.3 °C single reading or ≥38.0 °C sustained for 1 h

sections.p: The Multinational Association for Supportive Care (MASCC) score and the Clinical Index of Stable Febrile Neutropenia (CISFN) separate low‑risk from high‑risk patients.
b: MASCC ≥21 → low risk, may be managed outpatient
CISFN ≤2 → low risk; otherwise high risk

t.b: Answers: Is the patient low‑risk? A score ≥21 suggests outpatient therapy is safe
Answers: Is the patient clinically stable? Score ≤2 indicates low risk

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common precipitants are chemotherapy for solid tumours or leukaemia, HIV‑related marrow suppression, severe malaria, tuberculosis, and sickle‑cell disease crises.
b: Cytotoxic chemotherapy (especially alkylating agents, anthracyclines)
HIV infection with opportunistic marrow suppression
Severe malaria causing transient neutropenia
Disseminated TB with bone‑marrow involvement
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis with functional neutropenia

sections.p: Patients often appear acutely ill, with chills, rigors, or a new temperature spike. The physical exam may be deceptively quiet because neutropenia blunts classic signs of infection.
b: Fever or rigors without focal signs
Mucosal ulceration or oral thrush common in HIV
Possible skin lesions from malaria or bacterial entry

sections.p: Prioritise tests that guide antimicrobial choice and identify a source; adapt when labs are unavailable.

t.a: Blood cultures (2 sets, aerobic and anaerobic)
t.b: Detect bloodstream infection; positive culture directs targeted therapy
Answers: Is there a urinary source? Positive leukocyte esterase or nitrites suggest UTI
Answers: Is there pulmonary infection? Infiltrate supports pneumonia
Answers: Is malaria contributing? Positive test prompts antimalarial therapy

t.a: If culture unavailable: empirical broad‑spectrum coverage based on local flora
t.b: Answers: Which antibiotics to start? Choose agents covering Gram‑negatives, Pseudomonas, and anaerobes

sections.p: Rapid deterioration can occur from septic shock, invasive fungal infection, or hemorrhagic complications of marrow failure.
b: Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) or tachycardia >120 bpm
Respiratory distress or O₂ saturation <90 %
New mental status change
Persistent fever >72 h despite antibiotics

sections.p: Start empiric IV antibiotics within 60 minutes, adjust for risk, and consider adjuncts such as G‑CSF when indicated.
b: G‑CSF (filgrastim) for prolonged neutropenia (>7 days) or high‑risk regimens
Isolation precautions: hand hygiene, protective barrier, limit visitors

sections.p: Re‑assess daily, monitor ANC recovery, and modify chemotherapy schedules. Primary prophylaxis with G‑CSF for high‑risk regimens and vaccination where possible.
b: Daily temperature and ANC until ANC >500 µL and afebrile for 48 h
Educate patients on early fever reporting
Consider prophylactic flu and pneumococcal vaccines in HIV or cancer patients

sections.p: Febrile neutropenia can be mistaken for simple fever of unknown origin or for sepsis in a patient with normal neutrophils.
b: Fever of unknown origin (no neutropenia)
Septicemia in immunocompetent host (different antimicrobial spectrum)

sections.p: A normal white‑cell count does not exclude neutropenia if differential is not performed; malaria rapid tests can be false‑negative in low parasitaemia.
b: Relying on total WBC alone may miss neutropenia
Negative malaria test does not rule out infection in endemic areas

whenToSeekHelp: Fever lasting >72 h after appropriate antibiotics

faq.q: Why is fever alone enough to start antibiotics?
faq.a: Neutropenia blunts local signs, so fever is the earliest reliable indicator of infection.
In low‑risk patients (MASCC ≥21) who are haemodynamically stable, can tolerate oral intake, and have reliable follow‑up.
It shortens neutropenia duration, reducing infection risk, but is reserved for high‑risk or prolonged neutropenia.

exam: What is the definition of febrile neutropenia and why is the ANC threshold set at <500/µL? — Fever ≥38.3 °C (or ≥38.0 °C sustained) plus ANC <500 µL; <500 reflects markedly impaired bacterial defence.

A 45‑year‑old on cyclophosphamide presents with 38.5 °C fever and ANC 420/µL. What is your immediate management? — Start IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam) within 60 min, obtain cultures, assess risk.
How do you differentiate low‑risk from high‑risk febrile neutropenia in a resource‑limited setting? — Use MASCC score ≥21 or CISFN ≤2; low‑risk may be managed orally or outpatient.
Why is vancomycin added only in certain scenarios? — It covers MRSA and resistant Gram‑positives when there is a catheter, skin/soft‑tissue source, or hemodynamic instability.

A patient on ART for HIV develops fever and ANC 300/µL. Which additional infections should you consider? — Opportunistic infections such as disseminated TB, fungal infections, and malaria; obtain relevant tests.
When is G‑CSF indicated in febrile neutropenia? — For expected neutropenia >7 days, high‑risk chemotherapy regimens, or when rapid ANC recovery is needed.
What are the red‑flag signs that require ICU transfer? — Persistent hypotension, respiratory failure, altered consciousness, or uncontrolled sepsis despite antibiotics.
Explain why a normal total WBC does not exclude febrile neutropenia. — Neutrophil proportion may be low; a differential is required to calculate ANC.
